# linkfunctions7 <img src="man/figures/logo.png" align="right" height="139" alt="" />

In most R modeling packages a link function is a character string passed to a
fitting routine, which turns it internally into a few closures. Code outside
that package cannot use those closures, compute their higher derivatives, or
extend them without editing the package source.

`{linkfunctions7}` makes a link an object. Each constructor in the package
returns a link with exact analytical derivatives up to sixth order in both
directions, forward and inverse, and a diagnostic verifies those derivatives
against numerical ones.

It is part of [statmodels7](https://statmodels7.github.io), an S7 toolkit for
statistical modeling, and
[distributions7](https://statmodels7.github.io/distributions7/) uses it to
move between a constrained parameter and the unconstrained scale on which a
fitting routine works. The mathematics behind the formulas and the
derivations of the derivatives are worked out in
[the statmodels7 book](https://statmodels7.github.io/book/).

## Installation

```{r eval=FALSE}
# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("statmodels7/linkfunctions7")
```

Or install the whole toolkit at once:

```{r eval=FALSE}
pak::pak("statmodels7/statmodels7")
```

## A link is an object

Each link is created by a constructor and carries its own name, domain and
parameters. The forward link $\eta = g(\theta)$ and the inverse
$\theta = g^{-1}(\eta)$ are generics that dispatch on it, as are all ten
derivatives.

The softplus link illustrates why more than one positivity link is useful.
Like the log it keeps $\theta$ positive, but where the log implies an
exponential relationship everywhere, the softplus bends smoothly into a
straight line as $\eta$ grows, so a large linear predictor is not amplified
into an enormous parameter:

```{r}
softplus_link(a = 1)
plot(softplus_link(a = 1))
```

For a parameter confined to an interval, `bounded_link()` maps the
interval onto the whole real line and accepts a lower bound, an upper bound,
or both. For every link in the package the derivatives are closed-form
expressions, not finite differences, and they go to sixth order in both
directions:

```{r}
link <- bounded_link(lwr = -3, upr = 2)
theta <- linkinv(link, seq(-3, 3, length.out = 5))

theta                    # stays inside (-3, 2) whatever eta is
dlinkfun(link, theta)    # g'(theta), exactly
d6linkfun(link, theta)   # ... down to the sixth order
```

## A user-defined link

A link that the package does not ship is a subclass of `link()` with two
methods, `linkfun()` and `linkinv()`. The base class supplies the twelve
derivative generics by finite differences. Each fallback applies one central
stencil to the highest order that the link implements analytically, and
never a chain of first differences. The asymmetric family of Aranda-Ordaz
(1981), which contains the logit at $\alpha = 1$, needs only the two maps:

```{r}
ArandaOrdaz <- S7::new_class("ArandaOrdaz", parent = linkfunctions7::link)
S7::method(linkfun, ArandaOrdaz) <- function(x, theta) {
  a <- x@link_params$alpha
  log(((1 - theta)^(-a) - 1) / a)
}
S7::method(linkinv, ArandaOrdaz) <- function(x, eta) {
  a <- x@link_params$alpha
  1 - (1 + a * exp(eta))^(-1 / a)
}
ao_link <- function(alpha) {
  ArandaOrdaz(link_name = sprintf("aranda-ordaz(%g)", alpha),
              link_bounds = c(0, 1), link_params = list(alpha = alpha))
}
link_fallback_orders(ao_link(0.5))   # no analytic order in either direction
d2linkinv(ao_link(0.5), c(-1, 0, 1))
```

A method for any of the twelve derivative generics replaces its fallback, and
the orders above it are then differenced from that analytic order.
`link_fallback_orders()` reports the highest analytic order in each
direction.

## Validating a link

The derivatives are hand-written, so the package ships the tool that checks
them. `check_link()` confirms that a link inverts cleanly in both directions,
that it is strictly monotone, that the inverse function theorem
$g'(\theta)\,(g^{-1})'(\eta) = 1$ holds, and that every analytical derivative
agrees with a numerical one. It accepts any link and is most useful for a
newly written one:

```{r}
check_link(log_link())
```

An order that comes from a fallback is reported as numerical and is not
checked, because the check would then compare a finite difference with
another finite difference of the same function:

```{r}
check_link(ao_link(0.5))
```
